summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. Sexual-orientation discrimination was banned in 1996, making South Africa the first country to do so; marriage equality followed with the Civil Union Act of 2006; legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003; and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics.

The Western Cape stands under that national framework. Nothing in the sourced material identifies a Western Cape statute, prohibition, enforcement action or official directive restricting trans people. The province adds no criminalisation, no facility rule and no document rule of its own, so a trans visitor's exposure is governed by the national framework and by whoever operates the venue.

On 19 February 2025 Taswald Ruiters, a transgender woman from Eerste River, was threatened with removal from Green Point Athletic Stadium in Cape Town after using the women's bathroom. A security guard told her 'Look at you, you're a man', ordered her to use the men's bathroom and claimed he had the final say. Police were called four times and did not arrive in nearly three hours, MambaOnline reported on 28 February 2025. The stadium is a public facility operated by the City of Cape Town and was rented on the day by Western Province Athletics, which was responsible for the security services.

The confrontation records what a visibly trans visitor can meet at a public facility in the province's best-resourced metro: a removal attempt, explicit misgendering and an order to use the wrong facility, asserted by contracted security staff although no provincial rule restricts bathroom use by trans people. Police non-response over the full period of the incident means the escalation of such a dispute cannot be assumed to end quickly through official intervention.
tangentialFactors:
Responsibility for the stadium confrontation sat with a private security contractor engaged by the renting athletics body at a City of Cape Town venue, not with any Western Cape authority. Accountability for facility disputes in the province therefore attaches to venue operators and their contractors, and the absence of a provincial rule means the assertion of one rests on the individual guard's say-so.

The incident occurred at the best-resourced public facility in the province's principal metro, which has dedicated security staffing and repeated police call-outs available to it. Trans visitors to less well-served venues elsewhere in the Western Cape have less reason to expect a security or police response than was sought at Green Point, where four calls over nearly three hours produced no arrival.

The province's trans-specific exposure is behavioural rather than statutory: the barrier met at the stadium is enforcement without legal basis, whereas national law supplies the Equality Court route and the 2024 hate-crime protections against the same conduct.
localsOnly:
Residents of the Western Cape use the national Equality Court under PEPUDA for unfair discrimination claims; the sourced material shows no provincial equality body or provincial complaints route operating in its place.

Ruiters is a Western Cape resident rather than a visitor, and the confrontation took place at a municipal venue during ordinary local use of a public bathroom. The same exposure applies to residents' routine access to stadiums, changing rooms, clinics and municipal buildings across the province.

Legal gender recognition for residents proceeds under the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003, which is national legislation applied in the Western Cape. The sourced material identifies no Western Cape procedure, fee or waiting period layered on top of it.
outOfScopeNotes:

Unresolved: whether the security guard faced any disciplinary action, or whether any charge followed the incident, is not sourced. Only the threat of removal and the guard's statements during it are documented.

Unresolved: whether any of the four police calls produced a later arrival, a docket or an investigation is not sourced; the reported record ends with non-arrival in nearly three hours.
